source_text: ΣΥΓΚΡΙΣΙΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΙΚΗΣ ΔΥΝΑΣΤΕΙΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΛΟΥΤΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΕΡΟΧΗΣ, ΠΡΟΣ ΜΟΝΑΧΟΝ ΣΥΖΩΝΤΑ ΤΗ ΑΛΗΘΕΣΤΑΤΗ ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΝ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΙΑ. αʹ. Ὁρῶν ἐγὼ τοὺς πολλοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὰ δοκοῦντα εἶναι καλὰ μᾶλλον ἀγαπῶντάς τε καὶ θαυμάζοντας, ἢ τὰ φύσει χρηστὰ καὶ ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθὰ, ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι νομίζω περὶ ἑκατέρων βραχεῖς ποιήσασθαι τοὺς λόγους, καὶ παραθεῖναι νῦν ἀλλήλοις τά τε κατεῤῥᾳθυμημένα παρὰ πολλοῖς, τά τε πολλῆς τυγχάνοντα σπουδῆς, ἵνα μαθόντες τὸ διάφορον ἑκατέρων, τὰ μὲν ὡς ἄξια σπουδῆς καὶ σωτηρίας περὶ πολλοῦ ποιησώμεθα, τῶν δὲ καταφρονεῖν παιδευθῶμεν ὡς οὐδενὸς ἀξίων. Οὐκοῦν ἀγαπᾶται μὲν πλοῦτος καὶ δυναστεία καὶ ἀρχὴ καὶ δόξα, καὶ μακαρίζουσιν οἱ πολλοὶ τοὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν ἄρχοντας, φερομένους ἐπὶ λαμπρῶν ὀχημάτων, καὶ κηρύκων βοῆς ἀπολαύοντας καὶ δορυφορίας πολλῆς, καταπεφρόνηται δὲ τῶν φιλοσοφούντων ὁ βίος, καὶ τῶν τὴν μονήρη δίαιταν ᾑρημένων· κἀκεῖνοι μὲν φανέντες, πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιστρέφουσι τὸν δῆμον, οὗτοι δὲ φανέντες οὐδενὸς ὀφθαλμοὺς, ἢ κομιδῇ γε ὀλίγων, πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς ἕλκουσι. Καὶ τούτων μὲν οὐδεὶς ἂν ἐπιθυμήσειε γενέσθαι ὅμοιος, ἐκείνων δὲ ἅπαντες· καίτοι γε δυναστείαν μὲν κτήσασθαι, καὶ ἀρχὴν ἔθνους λαβεῖν, χαλεπόν τε καὶ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀδύνατον, καὶ πολλῶν ἂν δεηθεῖεν χρημάτων οἱ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐρασταί· τὸ δὲ μονήρη βίον ἑλέσθαι, καὶ τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ λατρείᾳ συζῇν, πᾶσιν ὁμοίως εὔπορόν τε καὶ ῥᾴδιον. Καὶ τῆς μὲν ἀρχῆς ἡ κτῆσις τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ συνδιαφθείρεται, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ζῶντας ἀπολιμπάνει τοὺς ἑαυτῆς ἐραστὰς, ἤδη δέ τινας καὶ εἰς κίνδυνον μέγαν ἢ ἀδοξίαν κατέστησεν· ὁ δὲ μονήρης βίος νῦν τε πολλῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀναπίμπλησι τοὺς δικαίους, καὶ μετὰ τὴν τοῦ βίου τελευτὴν λαμπροὺς καὶ χαίροντας ἐπὶ τὸ δικαστήριον ἄγει τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς, ὅτε τῶν ἀρξάντων οἱ πλείους μεγάλην ὀφθήσονται διδόντες τῶν βεβιωμένων τὴν δίκην. Φέρε δὴ παραθέντες ἀλλήλοις τά τε τῆς φιλοσοφίας ἀγαθὰ, τά τε δοκοῦντα εἶναι χρηστὰ τῆς ἐν τῷ παρόντι βίῳ δυναστείας καὶ δόξης, καταμάθωμεν τὸ διάφορον ἑκατέρων τῶν ἀγαθῶν· παράλληλα γὰρ ἔσται φανερώτερα· μᾶλλον δὲ, εἰ δοκεῖ, τὴν κορυφὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν, τὴν βασιλείαν λέγω, τῇ φιλοσοφίᾳ παραθέντες, θεωρήσωμεν ἑκατέρας κτήσεως τοὺς καρποὺς, καταμαθόντες ἀκριβῶς τίνων μὲν ὁ βασιλεὺς, τίνων δὲ ὁ φιλόσοφος ἄρχει. Οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν βασιλεὺς πόλεσι καὶ χώραις καὶ πολλοῖς ἐφέστηκεν ἔθνεσι, καὶ στρατηγοὺς καὶ ὑπάρχους καὶ στρατόπεδα καὶ δήμους καὶ βουλὰς τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ νεύμασιν ἄγων· ὁ δὲ Θεῷ δεδωκὼς ἑαυτὸν, καὶ τὸν μονήρη βίον ᾑρημένος, θυμοῦ καὶ φθόνου καὶ φιλαργυρίας καὶ ἡδονῆς καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἄρχει κακῶν, σκοπῶν ἀεὶ καὶ φροντίζων, ὅπως ἂν μὴ συγχωρήσειε τῇ ψυχῇ ὑπὸ τοῖς αἰσχροῖς γενέσθαι πάθεσι, μηδὲ δουλωθῆναι τὸν λογισμὸν τυραννίδι πικρᾷ, ἀλλ' ἀνωτέρω πάντων ἀεὶ τὴν διάνοιαν ἔχοι, τὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ φόβον ἐπιστήσας τοῖς πάθεσι. Τοιαύτην μὲν οὖν ὁ βασιλεὺς, τοιαύτην δὲ ὁ μοναχὸς ἀρχὴν καὶ δυναστείαν κέκτηται, ὥστε δικαιότερον ἄν τις τοῦτον βασιλέα καλέσειεν, ἢ τὸν ἁλουργίδι καὶ στεφάνῳ λαμπόμενον, καὶ καθήμενον ἐπὶ θρόνου χρυσοῦ. βʹ. Βασιλεὺς γὰρ ὡς ἀληθῶς ὁ θυμοῦ καὶ φθόνου καὶ ἡδονῆς κρατῶν, καὶ πάντα ὑπὸ τοὺς νόμους ἄγων τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τὸν νοῦν ἐλεύθερον τηρῶν, καὶ οὐκ ἐῶν ἐνδυναστεῦσαι τῇ ψυχῇ τὴν δεσποτείαν τῶν ἡδονῶν.
thought_title: True kingship is ruling the passions
orientation: John Chrysostom opens his treatise by comparing what most people admire—wealth, power, and kingship—with the monastic life, which he will argue is the truer kingship.
pass_a_gloss: Comparison of kingly power and wealth and preeminence, to a monk living with the truest way of life according to Christ. Chapter 1. Seeing I that the many of humans love and admire the things seeming to be good rather than the things by nature useful and truly good, necessary I consider it to be to make brief words about each, and to set side by side now with each other the things neglected by many and the things obtaining much zeal, so that having learned the difference of each, the one things as worthy of zeal and salvation we may value highly, and of the other things we may be taught to despise them as worthy of nothing. Therefore wealth is loved and power and rule and glory, and the many bless the rulers of the nations, carried on bright chariots, and enjoying the shout of heralds and much bodyguard, but the life of those practicing the way of life is despised, and of those having chosen the monastic way of life; and those when they appear turn the people toward themselves, but these when they appear draw toward themselves the eyes of no one, or at any rate of very few. And of these no one would desire to become like, but of those all men; and yet to acquire power, and to take rule of a nation, is hard and for the many impossible, and of much money would the lovers of rule have need; but to choose the monastic life, and to live with the service of God, is for all equally easy and easy. And of rule the acquisition is destroyed together with this life, but rather even while living it leaves behind its own lovers, and already some it has set into great danger or dishonor; but the monastic life now fills the just with many good things, and after the end of life leads them bright and rejoicing to the judgment seat of God and Father, when of those who ruled the majority will be seen paying the great penalty of the things lived. Come then, having set side by side with each other the good things of the way of life and the things seeming to be useful of the power and glory in the present life, let us learn the difference of each of the good things; for side by side they will be more evident; but rather, if it seems good, having set the summit of good things, kingship I mean, beside the way of life, let us observe the fruits of each acquisition, having learned accurately over what things the king rules and over what things the philosopher rules. Therefore the king stands over cities and lands and many nations, and leads generals and governors and armies and peoples and councils by his own nods; but the one having given himself to God, and having chosen the monastic life, rules anger and envy and love of money and pleasure and the other evils, watching always and taking care, how he might not allow the soul to come under the shameful passions, nor the reasoning to be enslaved to a bitter tyranny, but always keep the mind above all things, having set the fear of God over the passions. Such then rule and power the king, such the monk has acquired, so that more justly one would call this one king, than the one shining with purple and crown, and sitting on a golden throne. Chapter 2. For truly a king is the one ruling anger and envy and pleasure, and leading all things under the laws of God and keeping the mind free, and not allowing the despotism of pleasures to exercise power in the soul.

pass_b_english: A Comparison of Royal Power, Wealth, and Preeminence with the Monk Who Lives According to the Truest Way of Life in Christ. 1. I see that most people love and admire what merely seems good rather than what is naturally excellent and truly good. So I think it necessary to speak briefly about each kind, and to set side by side the things many people neglect and the things they pursue with great eagerness. Then, once we understand the difference between them, we may value the one as worthy of our effort and salvation, and learn to despise the other as worth nothing. People love wealth, power, rule, and glory, and most call the rulers of nations blessed as they ride on splendid chariots, enjoy the shouts of heralds, and are surrounded by a large bodyguard. But the way of life of those who practice it is despised, along with those who have chosen the monastic life. When those rulers appear, they turn the crowd toward themselves; when these monks appear, they draw no one's eyes to themselves, or at most very few. No one would wish to become like these, but everyone wishes to become like those. Yet to acquire power and take rule over a nation is difficult and impossible for most people, and lovers of rule would need great wealth. But to choose the monastic life and live in the service of God is equally easy and within reach for everyone. The possession of rule is destroyed together with this life; rather, it abandons its lovers even while they live, and has already brought some into great danger or disgrace. The monastic life, however, fills the righteous with many good things now, and after the end of life leads them radiant and rejoicing to the judgment seat of God the Father, when most rulers will be seen giving a great accounting for the lives they have lived. Come then, let us set side by side the good things of the way of life and the things that seem excellent in the power and glory of this present life, and let us learn the difference between each kind of good. For things placed side by side become clearer. Or rather, if it seems good, let us set the summit of good things—I mean kingship—beside the way of life, and observe the fruits of each possession, learning precisely over what the king rules and over what the monk rules. The king stands over cities, lands, and many nations, directing generals, governors, armies, peoples, and councils by his nods. But the one who has given himself to God and chosen the monastic life rules over anger, envy, love of money, pleasure, and the other evils, always watching and taking care that he does not allow his soul to come under shameful passions, nor his reason to be enslaved to a bitter tyranny, but keeps his mind always above all these things, setting the fear of God over the passions. Such is the rule and power the king possesses, and such is the rule and power the monk possesses, so that one would more justly call the monk a king than the one shining in purple and crown and seated on a golden throne. 2. For the true king is the one who masters anger, envy, and pleasure, who brings everything under the laws of God, keeps his mind free, and does not allow the tyranny of pleasures to exercise power in his soul.

problems.quote: the way of life of those who practice the monastic life is despised, along with those who have chosen the monastic way of life
problems.source_quote: καταπεφρόνηται δὲ τῶν φιλοσοφούντων ὁ βίος, καὶ τῶν τὴν μονήρη δίαιταν ᾑρημένων
problems.why: Source says 'the life of those who practice the way of life is despised, and those who have chosen the monastic life' — English reverses the glossary terms.
problems.fix: the way of life of those who practice it is despised, along with those who have chosen the monastic life
problems.ruling: Source: φιλοσοφούντων = philosophers/ascetics, not 'monastic life'; English conflates distinct terms.

problems.why: τῶν βεβιωμένων τὴν δίκην = 'giving account/reckoning for their lives', not 'paying a penalty'; δίκη here is 'reckoning, account, justice', not 'penalty'—they give an account, not necessarily pay.

refereed.quote: the way of life of those who practice it is despised, along with those who have chosen the monastic life
refereed.source_quote: καταπεφρόνηται δὲ τῶν φιλοσοφούντων ὁ βίος, καὶ τῶν τὴν μονήρη δίαιταν ᾑρημένων
refereed.why: Source says 'the life of those who practice philosophy is despised, and those who have chosen the monastic life'—two groups despised, not 'along with'.

refereed.quote: does not allow the tyranny of pleasures to exercise power in his soul
refereed.source_quote: καὶ οὐκ ἐῶν ἐνδυναστεῦσαι τῇ ψυχῇ τὴν δεσποτείαν τῶν ἡδονῶν
refereed.why: English says 'exercise power in his soul' but ἐνδυναστεῦσαι τῇ ψυχῇ means 'exercise power over the soul' (dative of disadvantage), not 'in'; agency flipped—pleasures don't dominate within soul but over it
refereed.fix: does not allow the tyranny of pleasures to exercise power over his soul
refereed.ruling: ἐνδυναστεῦσαι τῇ ψυχῇ: dative of disadvantage = 'over the soul,' not 'in his soul'; changes the domination relationship.
